description: A Single Mathematics B-style paper covering vector geometry, ODE models, Fourier coefficients, multivariable calculus, vector calculus, multiple integrals, and probability.
instructions: Show sufficient working to justify each answer.
Answers should be exact unless a numerical approximation is requested.
Begin each main question on a new page when working on paper.
label: Paper 1

questions.stem: Three beacons are fixed at \(A=(1,0,1)\), \(B=(3,1,2)\), and \(C=(2,-1,4)\). A probe moves on the line through \(P=(0,2,1)\) with direction vector \(\mathbf d=(1,-1,2)\).
questions.title: Probe Path and Observation Plane

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Write a vector equation for the probe line.
parts.answer: A line is determined by one point on the line and a non-zero direction vector. The probe passes through \(P=(0,2,1)\) and has direction \(\mathbf d=(1,-1,2)\). Therefore \[\mathbf r=(0,2,1)+s(1,-1,2),\qquad s\in\mathbb R.\] The parameter \(s\) selects the position of the probe along the path.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find a Cartesian equation of the plane through the three beacons.
parts.answer: Use two direction vectors in the beacon plane: \[\overrightarrow{AB}=B-A=(2,1,1),\qquad \overrightarrow{AC}=C-A=(1,-1,3).\] A normal vector is \[\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=(4,-5,-3).\] Hence the plane has equation \((4,-5,-3)\cdot(x,y,z)=d\). Substituting \(A=(1,0,1)\) gives \[d=4\cdot1-5\cdot0-3\cdot1=1.\] Therefore the Cartesian equation is \[4x-5y-3z=1.\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Find the acute angle between the probe line and the beacon plane.
parts.answer: Let \(\theta\) be the acute angle between the line and the plane, and let \(\mathbf n=(4,-5,-3)\) be a normal to the plane. The angle between a line and a plane satisfies \[\sin\theta=\frac{|\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf d|\,|\mathbf n|}.\] Here \[\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n=(1,-1,2)\cdot(4,-5,-3)=4+5-6=3,\] while \(|\mathbf d|=\sqrt6\) and \(|\mathbf n|=\sqrt{50}\). Thus \[\sin\theta=\frac{3}{\sqrt6\sqrt{50}}=\frac{\sqrt3}{10},\] so \[\theta=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{10}\right).\]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Find the volume of the tetrahedron with vertices \(A\), \(B\), \(C\), and \(P\).
parts.answer: Use the three edge vectors from \(A\): \[B-A=(2,1,1),\qquad C-A=(1,-1,3),\qquad P-A=(-1,2,0).\] The scalar triple product is \[(B-A)\cdot((C-A)\times(P-A)).\] Now \[(C-A)\times(P-A)=(-6,-3,1),\] and hence \[(2,1,1)\cdot(-6,-3,1)=-12-3+1=-14.\] The parallelepiped volume is \(14\), so the tetrahedron volume is \[\frac{14}{6}=\frac{7}{3}.\]

questions.stem: Answer the following independent questions on first-order and coupled differential equations.
questions.title: Cooling Model and Coupled Modes

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Solve \(\frac{dT}{dt}+\frac12T=10\), subject to \(T(0)=30\).
parts.answer: This is linear in standard form \(T'+\frac12T=10\). The integrating factor is \[\exp\int\frac12\,dt=e^{t/2}.\] Multiplying the equation by this factor gives \[\frac{d}{dt}\left(Te^{t/2}\right)=10e^{t/2}.\] Integrating, \[Te^{t/2}=20e^{t/2}+C,\] so \[T=20+Ce^{-t/2}.\] The initial condition gives \(30=20+C\), so \(C=10\). Therefore \[T(t)=20+10e^{-t/2}.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The coupled quantities \(u(t)\) and \(v(t)\) satisfy \(u'=2u-v\) and \(v'=u\). Deduce a second-order differential equation for \(u(t)\).
parts.answer: Differentiate \(u'=2u-v\) with respect to \(t\): \[u''=2u'-v'.\] Since \(v'=u\), this becomes \[u''=2u'-u.\] Moving all terms to the left gives the second-order equation \[u''-2u'+u=0.\] This equation contains only \(u\) and its derivatives.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Solve the equation from part (b), and describe the long-term behaviour when the coefficient of \(te^t\) is positive.
parts.answer: The auxiliary equation is \[r^2-2r+1=0,\] so \((r-1)^2=0\). The repeated root is \(r=1\), giving \[u(t)=(A+Bt)e^t.\] If \(B>0\), then the \(Bte^t\) term dominates for large \(t\). Thus \(u(t)\) grows without bound like \(Bte^t\).

questions.stem: Let \(f\) be the even \(2\pi\)-periodic function such that \(f(x)=2\) for \(0<x<\pi/2\) and \(f(x)=-1\) for \(\pi/2<x<\pi\). Values at jump points do not affect the Fourier coefficients.
questions.title: Shifted Pulse Fourier Series

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the symmetry of \(f\) and state which Fourier coefficients are zero.
parts.answer: The function is defined to be even, so \(f(-x)=f(x)\). Its Fourier series therefore contains only a constant term and cosine terms. All sine coefficients are zero: \[b_n=0\qquad(n\ge1).\] The graph is a repeated even pulse with height \(2\) near each multiple of \(2\pi\) and height \(-1\) near \(\pm\pi\).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the Fourier series of \(f\), giving the first four non-constant terms explicitly.
parts.answer: Because \(f\) is even, \[a_0=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\,dx=\frac{2}{\pi}\left(\int_0^{\pi/2}2\,dx+\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}(-1)\,dx\right)=1.\] For \(n\ge1\), \[a_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\left(\int_0^{\pi/2}2\cos nx\,dx+\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}(-1)\cos nx\,dx\right).\] Thus \[a_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\left(\frac{2\sin(n\pi/2)}{n}-\frac{\sin(n\pi)-\sin(n\pi/2)}{n}\right)=\frac{6}{\pi n}\sin\frac{n\pi}{2}.\] Hence \[f(x)\sim\frac12+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{6}{\pi n}\sin\frac{n\pi}{2}\cos nx.\] The first four non-constant terms are \[\frac{6}{\pi}\cos x-\frac{2}{\pi}\cos3x+\frac{6}{5\pi}\cos5x-\frac{6}{7\pi}\cos7x.\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Use Parseval's theorem to evaluate \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(2k+1)^2}\).
parts.answer: Parseval's theorem gives \[\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|f(x)|^2\,dx=\frac{a_0^2}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n^2.\] Since \(f\) is even, \[\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|f(x)|^2\,dx=\frac{2}{\pi}\left(\int_0^{\pi/2}4\,dx+\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}1\,dx\right)=5.\] Also \(a_0=1\), and only odd \(n\) contribute. Therefore \[5=\frac12+\frac{36}{\pi^2}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(2k+1)^2}.\] Rearranging gives \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(2k+1)^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{8}.\]

questions.stem: Let \(F(u,v)=f(x,y)\), where \(x=ue^v\) and \(y=ue^{-v}\). Assume \(f\) has continuous first partial derivatives.
questions.title: Coordinate Map and Directional Change

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find \(F_u\) and \(F_v\) in terms of partial derivatives of \(f\).
parts.answer: The partial derivatives of the coordinate map are \[x_u=e^v,\qquad y_u=e^{-v},\qquad x_v=ue^v,\qquad y_v=-ue^{-v}.\] The chain rule gives \[F_u=f_xx_u+f_yy_u=e^vf_x+e^{-v}f_y,\] and \[F_v=f_xx_v+f_yy_v=ue^vf_x-ue^{-v}f_y.\] The derivatives \(f_x\) and \(f_y\) are evaluated at \((x,y)=(ue^v,ue^{-v})\).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the Jacobian \(\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\) and state the local area scale at \((u,v)=(2,0)\).
parts.answer: The Jacobian is \[\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\begin{vmatrix}x_u&x_v\\y_u&y_v\end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix}e^v&ue^v\\e^{-v}&-ue^{-v}\end{vmatrix}.\] Thus \[\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=e^v(-ue^{-v})-(ue^v)(e^{-v})=-u-u=-2u.\] At \((u,v)=(2,0)\), the Jacobian is \(-4\). The local area scale is the absolute value, so small areas are scaled by a factor of \(4\).

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Let \(T(x,y)=x^2+3xy-y^2\) and \(G(u,v)=T(ue^v,ue^{-v})\). Find the directional derivative of \(G\) at \((1,0)\) in the direction \((3,4)\).
parts.answer: At \((u,v)=(1,0)\), the corresponding point is \((x,y)=(1,1)\). For \(T\), \[T_x=2x+3y,\qquad T_y=3x-2y.\] At \((1,1)\), \(T_x=5\) and \(T_y=1\). Using part (a) with \(u=1\), \(v=0\), \[G_u=5+1=6,\qquad G_v=5-1=4.\] The unit vector in the direction \((3,4)\) is \((3/5,4/5)\). Therefore \[D_{(3/5,4/5)}G(1,0)=(6,4)\cdot\left(\frac35,\frac45\right)=\frac{18}{5}+\frac{16}{5}=\frac{34}{5}.\]

questions.section: Section E: Critical Points and Vector Calculus
questions.stem: Consider the function \(f(x,y)=x^2+axy+4y^2\), where \(a\) is a real parameter, and the vector field \(\mathbf V=(x^2z,xy^2,yz^2)\).
questions.title: Parameter Surface and Curl

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: For \(a=2\), find and classify the critical point of \(f\).
parts.answer: When \(a=2\), \[f_x=2x+2y,\qquad f_y=2x+8y.\] Setting both first derivatives equal to zero gives \(2x+2y=0\), so \(x=-y\). Substituting into \(2x+8y=0\) gives \(-2y+8y=6y=0\), so \(y=0\) and \(x=0\). The Hessian is \[H=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&8\end{pmatrix}.\] Its determinant is \(16-4=12>0\), and \(f_{xx}=2>0\). Therefore \((0,0)\) is a local minimum.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the values of \(a\) for which \((0,0)\) is a strict local minimum of \(f\).
parts.answer: The Hessian matrix is \[H=\begin{pmatrix}2&a\\a&8\end{pmatrix}.\] For a strict local minimum of a quadratic form, this matrix must be positive definite. Since \(2>0\), the condition is that the determinant is positive: \[\det H=16-a^2>0.\] Therefore \[a^2<16,\qquad -4<a<4.\] Thus \((0,0)\) is a strict local minimum exactly for \(-4<a<4\).

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Compute \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf V\) and \(\nabla\times\mathbf V\).
parts.answer:
For \(\mathbf V=(P,Q,R)=(x^2z,xy^2,yz^2)\), the divergence is \[
abla\cdot\mathbf V=P_x+Q_y+R_z=2xz+2xy+2yz.\] The curl is \[
abla	imes\mathbf V=(R_y-Q_z,\ P_z-R_x,\ Q_x-P_y).\] Since \(R_y=z^2\), \(Q_z=0\), \(P_z=x^2\), \(R_x=0\), \(Q_x=y^2\), and \(P_y=0\), we get \[
abla	imes\mathbf V=(z^2,x^2,y^2).\]

questions.section: Section F: Multiple Integrals and Vector Identities
questions.stem: Let \(R\) be the region in the first quadrant bounded by \(y=x^2\) and \(y=3x\).
questions.title: Parabolic Region and Volume Moment

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe \(R\) using vertical slices and then by switching the order of integration.
parts.answer: The curves meet where \(x^2=3x\), so \(x=0\) or \(x=3\). With vertical slices, \[0\le x\le3,\qquad x^2\le y\le3x.\] To switch the order, note that \(y\) ranges from \(0\) to \(9\). The line \(y=3x\) gives \(x=y/3\), and the parabola \(y=x^2\) gives \(x=\sqrt y\) in the first quadrant. Hence \[0\le y\le9,\qquad \frac y3\le x\le\sqrt y.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Evaluate \(\iint_R y\,dA\) using the switched order from part (a).
parts.answer: Using the switched bounds, \[\iint_R y\,dA=\int_0^9\int_{y/3}^{\sqrt y}y\,dx\,dy.\] The inner integral is \[\int_{y/3}^{\sqrt y}y\,dx=y\left(\sqrt y-\frac y3\right)=y^{3/2}-\frac{y^2}{3}.\] Therefore \[\iint_R y\,dA=\int_0^9\left(y^{3/2}-\frac{y^2}{3}\right)dy=\left[\frac{2}{5}y^{5/2}-\frac{y^3}{9}\right]_0^9.\] Since \(9^{5/2}=243\), the value is \[\frac{486}{5}-81=\frac{81}{5}.\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Find the area of \(R\), and hence the \(y\)-coordinate of its centroid.
parts.answer: The area is \[A=\int_0^3(3x-x^2)\,dx=\left[\frac{3x^2}{2}-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^3=\frac{27}{2}-9=\frac92.\] The \(y\)-coordinate of the centroid is \[\bar y=\frac{1}{A}\iint_R y\,dA.\] Using part (b), \[\bar y=\frac{81/5}{9/2}=\frac{81}{5}\cdot\frac{2}{9}=\frac{18}{5}.\]

questions.stem: A laboratory tests detector modules from two suppliers and records rare warning events during repeated trials.
questions.title: Reliability Testing

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A module comes from supplier \(A\) with probability \(0.30\). The probability of failure is \(0.02\) for supplier \(A\) and \(0.05\) otherwise. If a module fails, find the probability that it came from supplier \(A\).
parts.answer: Let \(F\) be the failure event. The total probability of failure is \[P(F)=P(F\mid A)P(A)+P(F\mid A^c)P(A^c)=0.02(0.30)+0.05(0.70)=0.041.\] Bayes' theorem gives \[P(A\mid F)=\frac{P(F\mid A)P(A)}{P(F)}=\frac{0.02\cdot0.30}{0.041}=\frac{0.006}{0.041}=\frac{6}{41}.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A failed module is caught by an automatic screen with probability \(0.70\) and by an independent manual audit with probability \(0.20\). Find the probability that a failed module is released by both checks.
parts.answer: A failed module is released only if it is not caught by the screen and not caught by the audit. The two checks are independent, so \[P(\hbox{released}\mid F)=(1-0.70)(1-0.20)=0.30\cdot0.80=0.24.\] Thus \(24\%\) of failed modules are expected to pass both checks under this model.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: In a separate run, \(900\) independent modules each produce a rare warning with probability \(0.004\). Use a Poisson approximation to estimate the probability of at most two warnings.
parts.answer: Let \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(900,0.004)\). Since \(n\) is large and \(p\) is small, use a Poisson approximation with \[\lambda=np=900(0.004)=3.6.\] Therefore \[P(X\le2)\approx e^{-3.6}\left(1+3.6+\frac{3.6^2}{2}\right).\] Since \(3.6^2/2=6.48\), this is \[11.08e^{-3.6}\approx0.303.\]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Weekly warning counts have mean \(3.6\) and variance \(3.6\). For \(50\) independent weeks, estimate \(P(\bar X>4.0)\).
parts.answer: For the sample mean, \[E[\bar X]=3.6,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{3.6}{50}=0.072.\] Hence the standard deviation of \(\bar X\) is \(\sqrt{0.072}\approx0.268\). Using a normal approximation, \[P(\bar X>4.0)\approx P\left(Z>\frac{4.0-3.6}{0.268}\right)=P(Z>1.49).\] From standard normal tables this is approximately \(0.068\).
